newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar basks in economic success.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar basks in economic success.

text.p: A year after coming to power, Spain's conservative government is winning praise for cleaning up an economy once considered second rate.

The Popular Party, which formed the centre-right government on May 5, 1996, has delivered dramatic declines in interest rates, inflation and public expenditure that have won the respect of friend and foe alike.

But its sure-footed economic policy has often contrasted sharply with unpopular political stands, which have heightened public suspicion of a party whose roots lie in the four-decade dictatorship that ended with the death of Francisco Franco in 1975.

And so the government, on the eve of its anniversary, is trumpeting the accomplishments of its economic programme -- a gradualist pursuit of free market concepts that blends privatisation, deregulation and budget orthodoxy.
In late April, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar called a news conference to take advantage of favourable European Union Commission forecasts on Spain's drive to join Europe's single currency.
The EU said Spain in 1997 would narrow the state budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product -- the single currency benchmark -- from 4.4 percent in 1996 and 6.6 percent in 1995.
"The was clear backing to the Spanish economy and to the economic policy the government is developing," Aznar said.

Although part of the improvement must be attributed to past governments and to a Europe-wide economic effort, foreign observers particularly note the government's accomplished handling of financial markets.
"After just a short period, international financial markets gave the government their trust," a western diplomat said.

"The government has convinced the markets that they are serious (on the deficit and privatisations). They've been strong on sticking to the deficit target. Markets see that and the reward is lower rates and a stable peseta."
Inflation dropped to 2.2 percent in March, its lowest level in 29 years and a sharp improvement from January's 2.9 percent.
This progress, plus government pledges to bring down the debt burden and cut the deficit, have steadied the peseta and brought long-term rates down.

As a result, the government, which has made joining Europe's Economic and Monetary Union at launch in 1999 its overriding economic goal, now meets three of the five criteria -- on inflation, currency stability and long-term rates.
"We have passed from not fulfilling any criterion one year ago to meeting three out of five," Aznar said.
"I am convinced at the end of this year Spain will meet comfortably and with rigour and security these targets, and that we'll be a part of the leading countries," he said.
But perhaps the most telling sign of the government's success has been its ability to reduce an obscure indicator called the yield spread.
The difference in yield between Spanish bonds and their sturdier German counterparts has narrowed sharply, suggesting that the extra risk in holding Spanish debt no longer warranted such a premium.
Spanish yields dropped in January to only 83/100ths of a percent above German Bunds. In March 1996 the premium was 330 basis points and in the summer of 1995 it was 500 points.
The government itself seems at times bemused by its success.

"Those economic goals (from last year) are now so real that it seems that we weren't ambitious, but you have to consider where we were in 1996. Not one expert believed we could do it with inflation and long-term rates but... we beat the models," Economic Secretary Cristobal Montoro told journalists.

But the improvement is very tangible and Spanish citizens are giving the government high marks for its economic work, although this rating does not spill over into an overly favourable assessment of its politics.

"Those citizens that see a positive evolution in the economy are double those who perceive a worsening, and for the first time, a significant percentage of Spaniards (14 percent) said they had noticed improvement in their financial conditions," said a poll in the newspaper El Pais late in April.
"(But) the assessment of economic policy does not result in improved ratings overall for the government which continues to earn just a passing grade," it said.

Spaniards are displeased with the government's new hard-line stance toward Cuba and its decision last summer against opening secret files that could implicate the former government in the 1980s "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas, another poll showed.
But Aznar has tied his political future to the success of Spain's economic policy. If Spain join the EMU launch, he may call early elections.

"The cardinal goal of this government is entry into EMU and should this goal be reached in April/May 1998, there is speculation Aznar will call early elections in order to win an absolute parliamentary majority," another western diplomat said.
"His chances aren't bad, since he can underpin his successes with numbers."
